title: Read the landscape. Follow the air.
learning_goal: Explain how moisture direction and a mountain barrier can produce contrasting rainfall, and apply the explanation at another place.

sources.title: NCERT Climate / IIT Kanpur
sources.supports: Windward Western Ghats and leeward plateau differ during the southwest monsoon.

sources.title: Met Office
sources.supports: Ascent, condensation/precipitation and descending-air warming explain important mountain weather effects.

sources.title: NASA Earth Observatory
sources.supports: Eastern Andean slopes receive moisture from the continental interior; the western Atacama side is dry.

steps.title: Two places. One mountain barrier.
steps.question: Which side usually receives more rain during southwest monsoon conditions: cyan A on the coast or amber B toward Pune? Explain why.
steps.narration: Look at the two rings. Cyan A is on the coast. Amber B is inland near Pune. During the southwest monsoon, which side would usually receive more rain, and why? Type your answer here in Nara.
steps.follow_up: What happens to moist air as it approaches and climbs over the mountains? Connect that process to your choice.
steps.visual_note: Real Earth terrain; rings and airflow are schematic teaching aids, not weather observations.
hints: Moist southwest monsoon air approaches from the Arabian Sea. Which side meets it before it crosses the ridge?
Rising air cools. What could happen to water vapour as the air cools?

rubric.expected: A, the incoming coastal/windward side is favoured for rainfall.
reasoning: Moist air approaches from the Arabian Sea.
The barrier forces air upward; cooling and condensation favour precipitation on incoming slopes.
The leeward inland side is often comparatively drier.
misconceptions: Mountains attract rain without changing the air.
The inland side always gets more because it is east.

explanation.title: First, follow the incoming moisture.
explanation.text: Moist monsoon air arrives from the Arabian Sea and meets the Western Ghats. The terrain forces part of that flow upward.
explanation.narration: Start at the sea. Follow the cyan schematic arrow toward the ridge. The mountains force moist air to rise.

explanation.title: As air rises, it cools.
explanation.text: Cooling can bring the air to saturation. Condensation, cloud formation and precipitation favour the incoming slopes, explaining why A is often wetter.
explanation.narration: As the air rises, it cools. Water vapour can condense into cloud droplets, and precipitation is favoured on the incoming slopes.

explanation.title: Now look beyond the ridge.
explanation.text: The inland side is often drier after moisture has been lost. Descending air may also warm. This is a seasonal contrast, not a claim that Pune never gets rain.
explanation.narration: Beyond the ridge, air has often lost some moisture. As it descends it can warm. The inland side is comparatively drier. Now let us test the same idea at a different mountain range.

steps.title: Same idea. A different direction.
steps.time_context: Moist easterly flow example; not every season or the whole Andes
steps.question: Here, moisture approaches from the continental interior to the EAST. Which side faces that air: cyan A in the west, or amber B on the eastern slopes? Explain the mountain process.
steps.narration: We are now at the central Andes. In this example, moisture approaches from the east. Cyan A is west of the range and amber B is east. Which side faces the moist air, and what happens as that air climbs?
steps.follow_up: Explain why that slope is favoured. Connect the incoming direction with rising air, cooling and rainfall.
steps.visual_note: Central Andes example; schematic airflow and location rings. Southern Patagonia has a different prevailing-wind pattern.
hints: Start east of the ridge and trace the incoming moist flow. Which slope makes it climb first?

rubric.expected: B, the eastern slopes meet the incoming moisture in this example.
reasoning: Recognizes moisture approaches from the east in this central Andes setting.
Applies uplift/cooling and precipitation to the eastern incoming side.
Does not treat a fixed compass direction as universally wetter.
misconceptions: The western side must always be wetter because it was correct in India.
All of the Andes share one wind direction.

explanation.title: B faces the incoming moisture.
explanation.text: In this central Andes example, moisture arrives from the eastern continental interior and is lifted on the eastern slopes. The western Atacama side is much drier.
explanation.narration: This time, B is the incoming side. Moisture arrives from the eastern continental interior and rises on the eastern slopes. The expected choice has changed, but the mechanism has not.

explanation.title: Windward is a relationship.
explanation.text: Ask where the moisture comes from and which slope it meets first. Do not memorize west or east. Terrain is one part of a climate system with several interacting causes.
explanation.narration: Windward means facing the incoming wind. In Maharashtra it was the western side. Here it is the eastern side. Follow the air and use the mechanism. Do not memorize a compass direction.
